title: Scalar Variables - Single Values
description: Learn to store and retrieve single values using scalar variables with ${...} syntax.

theory.title: Scalar Variables: Storing Single Values
theory.content:
MENTOR-9's display shifts to show a memory bank interface.

"PROTO-7, your sequencing works. But tests need data—and data needs storage. That's what variables are for. Let's start with the simplest type: scalar variables."

What is a Variable?

A variable is a named storage location that holds a value. Think of it like a labeled box:

  • The box has a name (the variable name)
  • Inside the box is a value (the data)
  • You can store new values
  • You can retrieve the value anytime

Scalar Variables

A scalar variable holds a single value. It could be:

  • A string: "Navigation System"
  • A number: 42
  • A boolean: True or False
  • Any single piece of data

In Robot Framework, scalar variables use the ${variable_name} syntax.

Basic Syntax

*** Test Cases ***
Variable Example
    ${name}    Set Variable    Robot Framework
    Log        ${name}

What happens:

  1. ${name} is created and assigned the value "Robot Framework"
  2. Log ${name} outputs: "Robot Framework"

The Set Variable Keyword

The Set Variable keyword assigns a value to a variable:

${variable}    Set Variable    value

Components:

  • ${variable} - The variable name (on the left)
  • Set Variable - The keyword that does the assignment
  • value - The value to store (can be text, number, etc.)

Why Use Variables?

BenefitExample
Reusability Store API URL once, use it in 10 tests
Maintainability Change username in one place, affects all tests
Readability ${max_retries} is clearer than the number 3
Dynamic values Store API response, use it in next request

Logging Variables

Two ways to display variable values:

*** Test Cases ***
Logging Demo
    ${ship}    Set Variable    Starlight Explorer
    
    # Method 1: Embed in Log message
    Log    Ship name: ${ship}
    
    # Method 2: Use Log Variable (shows name and value)
    Log Variable    ${ship}

Output:

Method 1: "Ship name: Starlight Explorer"
Method 2: "${ship} = Starlight Explorer"

Log Variable is useful for debugging because it shows both the variable name and its value.

Multiple Variables

You can create as many variables as needed:

*** Test Cases ***
Multiple Variables
    ${username}    Set Variable    admin@example.com
    ${password}    Set Variable    SecurePass123
    ${url}         Set Variable    https://api.example.com
    
    Log    Logging in as ${username}
    Log    API endpoint: ${url}

Variable Naming Rules

Valid variable names:

  • ✅ ${my_var} - Underscores allowed
  • ✅ ${MyVar} - Camel case allowed
  • ✅ ${MY_VAR} - All caps allowed
  • ✅ ${my var} - Spaces allowed (unusual but valid!)
  • ✅ ${var123} - Numbers allowed (not at start)

Invalid variable names:

  • ❌ ${my-var} - Hyphens NOT allowed
  • ❌ ${123var} - Can't start with number
  • ❌ ${my.var} - Dots have special meaning (dictionary access)

Important: Variable names are case-sensitive!

  • ${myVar} is different from ${MyVar}
  • ${myVar} is different from ${MYVAR}

Real-World Example: API Testing

*** Test Cases ***
Get User Data
    ${base_url}    Set Variable    https://api.github.com
    ${username}    Set Variable    robotframework
    ${endpoint}    Set Variable    ${base_url}/users/${username}
    
    Log    Fetching user: ${username}
    Log    From endpoint: ${endpoint}
    # Output: From endpoint: https://api.github.com/users/robotframework

Notice how ${endpoint} uses other variables inside its value. Variables can reference other variables!

MENTOR-9: "Now test your memory banks. Create variables for a ship system name and its status. Store them, then log them. Show me your circuits can remember."
